title: When did we start walking for leisure“
paragraphs: 'Going for a walk' is a popular pastime among older and younger generations alike because of its well-known benefits for our physical and mental health. But you may be surprised to hear that meandering through pretty streets or hiking along mountainous ridges have not always been considered leisure activities, according to Daniel Gale, a researcher of pedestrianism.

He says that in Britain, walking for fun "wasn't really a thing" until the 1780s. Before that, it was just something people did out of necessity, and some people associated it with criminal activity. But for Charles Dickens, the famous English 19th Century author, marching through London streets and tramping around the countryside was a big part of the creative process; a time to absorb what was going on around him. He walked at an impressive pace of four miles per hour, according to his biography by Peter Ackroyd.

But if speed-walking isn't your thing, perhaps you can take inspiration from another big-thinking wanderer. 19th Century American writer Henry David Thoreau took a slower approach, preferring to saunter over hills and fields and meander through the woods. He said that he could not preserve his health and spirits, unless he spent four hours a day walking at least.

This idea of taking a stroll to clear your head has survived through to the 21st Century, but has pedestrian etiquette remained the same? A 1780 article for the London Magazine advised pedestrians to avoid things such as loitering in conversation and obstructing people behind you with a "sauntering gait".

Nowadays, we could probably add distracted phone-users to that list. In this modern age, when many of us are tied to our desks and to our screens, the simple act of stepping out onto the city pavements, or getting lost in nature, may make all the difference to our wellbeing. Whether you see yourself more as a casual stroller or a purposeful strider, why not build a habit out of it?

vocabulary.entry: **meander** /miˈændə(r)/ v. 蜿蜒漫步，闲逛（书面语）
vocabulary.example: We spent the afternoon meandering through the old town.
vocabulary.translation: 我们整个下午都在老城区闲逛。

vocabulary.entry: **pedestrianism** /pəˈdestriənɪzəm/ n. 步行运动，徒步运动（专业术语，书面语）
vocabulary.example: Pedestrianism became a popular recreational activity in the 19th century.
vocabulary.translation: 步行运动在19世纪成为一项受欢迎的娱乐活动。

vocabulary.entry: **necessity** /nəˈsesəti/ n. 需要，必要性（书面语）
vocabulary.example: He only left his home out of necessity.
vocabulary.translation: 他只在不得已时才离开家。

vocabulary.example: People often associate walking with leisure.
vocabulary.translation: 人们常将步行与休闲联系在一起。

vocabulary.example: He marched up the stairs without saying a word.
vocabulary.translation: 他一言不发地大步走上楼梯。

vocabulary.entry: **tramp** /træmp/ v. 徒步行走，跋涉（书面语）
vocabulary.example: They spent the day tramping through the countryside.
vocabulary.translation: 他们一整天都在乡间徒步行走。

vocabulary.entry: **impressive** /ɪmˈpresɪv/ adj. 令人印象深刻的，惊人的
vocabulary.example: The view from the top of the mountain was impressive.
vocabulary.translation: 从山顶看到的景色令人印象深刻。

vocabulary.example: He walked at a brisk pace.
vocabulary.translation: 他轻快地走着。

vocabulary.entry: **wanderer** /ˈwɒndərə(r)/ n. 漫游者，徘徊者（书面语）
vocabulary.example: He was a wanderer who never stayed in one place for long.
vocabulary.translation: 他是一个漫游者，从不在一个地方久留。

vocabulary.example: The beautiful scenery provided the inspiration for his painting.
vocabulary.translation: 美丽的景色为他的画作提供了灵感。

vocabulary.example: He sauntered down the street with his hands in his pockets.
vocabulary.translation: 他双手插在口袋里，沿着街道闲逛。

vocabulary.example: They went for a stroll in the park.
vocabulary.translation: 他们去公园散步了。

vocabulary.entry: **clear one's head** /ˌklɪə wʌnz ˈhed/ phr. 理清思绪，使头脑清醒（固定表达）
vocabulary.example: A walk in the fresh air helped clear my head.
vocabulary.translation: 在新鲜空气中散步有助于我理清思绪。

vocabulary.entry: **pedestrian etiquette** /pəˈdestriən ˈetɪket/ n. 步行礼仪（固定表达）
vocabulary.example: Pedestrian etiquette includes not blocking the path for others.
vocabulary.translation: 步行礼仪包括不挡住他人的路。

vocabulary.example: The path is used by both pedestrians and cyclists.
vocabulary.translation: 这条路行人和骑行者都会使用。

vocabulary.example: Teenagers were loitering outside the shop.
vocabulary.translation: 青少年们在商店外面闲逛。

vocabulary.example: A fallen tree was obstructing the road.
vocabulary.translation: 一棵倒下的树挡住了路。

vocabulary.example: He walked with a slow, shuffling gait.
vocabulary.translation: 他走路缓慢，拖着脚步。

vocabulary.entry: **distracted** /dɪˈstræktɪd/ adj. 分心的，注意力分散的
vocabulary.example: He seemed distracted during the meeting.
vocabulary.translation: 他在会议期间似乎心不在焉。

vocabulary.entry: **tied to** /taɪd tu/ phr. 束缚于，受……限制（固定表达）
vocabulary.example: Many workers are tied to their desks for most of the day.
vocabulary.translation: 许多工人一天大部分时间都被束缚在办公桌前。

vocabulary.example: He was walking along the pavement when the car hit him.
vocabulary.translation: 他正沿着人行道行走时，那辆车撞到了他。

vocabulary.entry: **wellbeing** /ˈwelbiːɪŋ/ n. 健康，幸福，福祉（书面语）
vocabulary.example: We try to ensure that all our employees have a sense of wellbeing.
vocabulary.translation: 我们努力确保所有员工都有幸福感。

vocabulary.example: He wore casual clothes to the party.
vocabulary.translation: 他穿着休闲装参加派对。

vocabulary.example: The park is popular with strollers and dog walkers.
vocabulary.translation: 这个公园很受散步者和遛狗者的欢迎。

vocabulary.entry: **purposeful** /ˈpɜːpəsfl/ adj. 有目的的，坚定的（书面语）
vocabulary.example: She walked with a purposeful stride.
vocabulary.translation: 她迈着坚定的步伐走着。

vocabulary.example: He was a fast strider and soon left us behind.
vocabulary.translation: 他走得很快，很快就把我们甩在后面了。

sentences.english: 'Going for a walk' is a popular pastime among older and younger generations alike because of its well-known benefits for our physical and mental health.
sentences.chinese: "去散步"是受老年人和年轻人欢迎的休闲方式，因为它对我们的身心健康有着众所周知的好处。

sentences.english: But you may be surprised to hear that meandering through pretty streets or hiking along mountainous ridges have not always been considered leisure activities, according to Daniel Gale, a researcher of pedestrianism.
sentences.chinese: 但根据步行运动研究者丹尼尔·盖尔的说法，听到漫步于美丽的街道或沿着山脊徒步并非一直被视为休闲活动，你可能会感到惊讶。

sentences.english: He says that in Britain, walking for fun "wasn't really a thing" until the 1780s.
sentences.chinese: 他说，在英国，为乐趣而散步直到18世纪80年代才真正流行起来。

sentences.english: Before that, it was just something people did out of necessity, and some people associated it with criminal activity.
sentences.chinese: 在此之前，散步只是人们出于需要而做的事，有些人还将其与犯罪活动联系在一起。

sentences.english: But for Charles Dickens, the famous English 19th Century author, marching through London streets and tramping around the countryside was a big part of the creative process; a time to absorb what was going on around him.
sentences.chinese: 但对于19世纪英国著名作家查尔斯·狄更斯来说，快步行走于伦敦街头和在乡间徒步是创作过程中的重要部分；是了解周围事物发生的时刻。

sentences.english: He walked at an impressive pace of four miles per hour, according to his biography by Peter Ackroyd.
sentences.chinese: 根据彼得·阿克罗伊德的传记，他以每小时四英里的惊人速度行走。

sentences.english: But if speed-walking isn't your thing, perhaps you can take inspiration from another big-thinking wanderer.
sentences.chinese: 但如果快走不是你的风格，也许你可以从另一位深思熟虑的漫步者那里获得灵感。

sentences.english: 19th Century American writer Henry David Thoreau took a slower approach, preferring to saunter over hills and fields and meander through the woods.
sentences.chinese: 19世纪美国作家亨利·戴维·梭罗采用了较慢的方式，更喜欢在丘陵和田野间闲逛，在树林中蜿蜒漫步。

sentences.english: He said that he could not preserve his health and spirits, unless he spent four hours a day walking at least.
sentences.chinese: 他说，除非每天至少步行四个小时，否则他无法保持健康和活力。

sentences.english: This idea of taking a stroll to clear your head has survived through to the 21st Century, but has pedestrian etiquette remained the same?
sentences.chinese: 这种通过散步来使头脑清醒的观点一直延续到了21世纪，但步行礼仪是否保持不变呢？

sentences.english: A 1780 article for the London Magazine advised pedestrians to avoid things such as loitering in conversation and obstructing people behind you with a "sauntering gait".
sentences.chinese: 1780年《伦敦杂志》的一篇文章建议行人避免诸如在交谈中闲逛，以及用"漫步的步态"阻挡身后的人。

sentences.english: Nowadays, we could probably add distracted phone-users to that list.
sentences.chinese: 如今，我们可能还要把分心的手机使用者添加到这个清单中。

sentences.english: In this modern age, when many of us are tied to our desks and to our screens, the simple act of stepping out onto the city pavements, or getting lost in nature, may make all the difference to our wellbeing.
sentences.chinese: 在这个现代时代，当我们许多人被束缚在办公桌和屏幕前时，走到城市的人行道上，或者迷失在大自然中，这一简单举动可能对我们的福祉产生重大影响。

sentences.english: Whether you see yourself more as a casual stroller or a purposeful strider, why not build a habit out of it?
sentences.chinese: 无论你视自己为随意的漫步者还是目标明确的大步行走者，何不将它养成一种习惯呢？
